newsitem.title: USA: Iowa county to seek IRS ruling for casino sale.
newsitem.headline: Iowa county to seek IRS ruling for casino sale.

text.p: - Polk County, Iowa, will seek a private letter ruling from the U.S. Internal Revenue Service to determine whether it could sell a race track and casino that were financed by tax-exempt bonds, a county official said Tuesday.

"Our attorney has advised us he will not issue an opinion that we can sell the facility until we have a revenue ruling that says it won't jeopardize the tax-exempt status of the bonds," said Norman Jesse, the county's manager of development.
Jesse said a decision from the IRS could take six to nine months.

If the ruling gives the county the green light to sell the successful Prairie Meadows Race Track and Casino in Altoona, Jesse said county officials would then determine if a sale would be "in the best interest of the public we represent."

Although a possible sale of the race track-casino is moot for several months, Circus Circus Enterprises Inc, a Las Vegas-based gambling company, unveiled a plan Tuesday to purchase the facility from the county.
The public relations office for Circus Circus declined to release any information from a media briefing held in Iowa.
However, information obtained by Polk County indicates that the company would provide at least $250 million to the Racing Association of Central Iowa to buy the facility from the county.
In return, Circus Circus would be paid a 50 percent management fee out of Prairie Meadows' profits and would plan to add a hotel and other improvements to the facility.
Jesse said Circus Circus had not made any presentation to county officials.
Stephen Rosholt, a partner at the Minneapolis law firm of Faegre & Benson, the county's bond counsel, said Tuesday that the letter ruling request should be filed within the next two weeks.
He said the request is predicated on an IRS revenue procedure dealing with the sale of property financed by tax-exempt bonds within five years of the issuance of bonds.
Polk County originally issued $40 million of bonds to build Prairie Meadows in 1984. Three years later, the bonds were remarketed under a lease-purchase agreement.

A subsequent bankruptcy of the race track allowed the county to issue $38.8 million of tax-exempt general obligation bonds in 1993 to redeem the outstanding bonds and take control of the facility from the Racing Association of Central Iowa, which had owned and operated the track under the lease-purchase agreement.
Just last year, the county issued $26 million of bonds to install slot machines at Prairie Meadows.
The addition of the slot machines has turned the facility into a gold mine for the county. Jesse said Prairie Meadows is generating $5 million in revenues a month for the county.
